text: A rival is someone you are competing against for the same thing: the same prize, the same customers, the same spot on the team. The word hints that the competition is close and long-running. Mars is called a rival here because it and Mondelez are two giant food companies going after the same shoppers in the same snack aisle.

To migrate is to move from one place to another. You have probably met the word with birds flying south for winter, but scientists use it for anything that shifts position, including water. Here it means water spreads out of the damp parts of a snack and into the dry parts, until the crunchy bits go soft.

To amplify something is to make it bigger, louder or stronger. An amplifier does that to sound, turning the tiny signal from an electric guitar into something loud enough to fill a hall. The nutritionist means snacks are now built to amplify the whole experience of eating, piling on crunch and crackle on top of flavour.

A trend is a change that keeps going the same direction over time, rather than a one-off. Spotting one means noticing that lots of separate things are drifting the same way. Here the trend is that snack after snack is being made crunchier or chewier on purpose.

Texture is what something feels like to touch, or in the case of food, what it feels like in your mouth and how it behaves when you bite it. Crunchy, chewy, gooey and creamy are all textures, not flavours. This whole article is about food companies competing on texture instead of taste.

Novelty is newness: the quality of being something people have not seen before. The related adjective is novel, meaning new and unfamiliar. The article says the novelty in snacks now comes from texture, because so few genuinely novel flavours are left to try.

In a story about business, a giant is not a creature from a fairy tale. It means a company so large that it shapes a whole industry. Calling Mondelez one food giant is a quick way of saying it is among the biggest food companies in the world.

Mondelez is one of the biggest snack companies on earth, based in America. It owns Cadbury, Oreo, Ritz and Toblerone, among many others, so a lot of brands that look unrelated on the shelf belong to the same owner. Dairy Milk, the bar discussed here, is one of its Cadbury products.

Lotus Biscoff is a Belgian brand of thin, spiced caramel biscuit, often handed out with coffee on planes. It also comes as a spreadable paste made from the crushed biscuits. Both the biscuit and the spread were built into the chocolate bar described here.

Mars here is not the planet but the American company, one of the largest sweet makers in the world and still owned by the Mars family. It makes M and M's, Snickers, Skittles and Milky Way. It is Mondelez's closest competitor in snacks.

Big food is a nickname for the handful of enormous companies that make most of the packaged food in supermarkets. Writers use the Big pattern for other industries too: big tech, big oil, big pharma. It usually carries a note of suspicion about how much power those few companies hold.

Engineers design and build things, so to engineer something is to design it carefully and deliberately rather than letting it happen. You can engineer a bridge, but also a snack or a situation. Saying big food has engineered every aspect of snacks means nothing about them is accidental, down to the colour of the wrapper.

Moreish is a British word for food so pleasant that one is never enough and you keep going back for more. There is no neat American equivalent, which is why you will meet it mostly in British writing. It is exactly what snack makers are aiming for.

An aroma is a smell, and almost always a pleasant one, especially from food or drink. You would say the aroma of fresh bread, not the aroma of a locker room. The article points out that the aroma released when a packet is torn open was designed on purpose.

Mouthfeel is a food industry term for how something feels inside your mouth, separate from how it tastes. Creamy, gritty, sticky, fizzy and dry are all mouthfeel. The word exists because flavour alone cannot describe why one chocolate is pleasant and another is waxy.

Mintel is a company that studies what shoppers buy and want, then sells those findings to businesses. The numbers in this article about texture claims and demand come from its work. It is one of the firms big food pays to tell it which way tastes are turning.

A research firm is a company whose product is information. It surveys shoppers, counts sales and tracks what people say online, then sells the results to other companies that want to know what is happening. When an article quotes a percentage about shoppers, a firm like this usually measured it.

To reckon is to work something out or judge it: to calculate, estimate or believe. British writers use it where Americans would say thinks or estimates. Mintel reckons the share of snacks grew, meaning that is its best estimate rather than an exact count.

A share is a part of a whole, so the share of something is the slice of the total that fits a description, usually given as a percentage. The share of snacks making texture claims went from 31% to 41%, meaning 41 out of every 100 snacks did. The number of snacks overall could have changed too, which is why shares and totals are different measurements.

To cook something up is to invent or produce it, often with a hint of effort or scheming: to cook up a plan, to cook up an excuse. Saying texture can be hard to cook up is a small joke, because here the thing being invented really is food. It means getting the texture right is difficult work.

Research and development, usually shortened to R and D, is the department inside a company that works out new products and improves existing ones. Research is finding out how things behave; development is turning that into something that can be made a million times over. Nearly every large company has one, and so do universities and governments.

To point something out is to draw attention to a fact, especially one others may have missed or overlooked. It suggests the thing is true and simply needed saying. Writers use it to introduce an expert's remark, as it does here with the head of research.

Moist means slightly wet: damp, but pleasantly so rather than soaking. Cake is meant to be moist, a towel after a shower is wet. In food science it matters because water moves out of moist ingredients into dry ones.

Crisp food is dry and firm and breaks with a snap, like a cracker or a fresh apple. The opposite is soggy, which is what crisp things become once water gets into them. In British English crisps are also what Americans call potato chips, but here crisp is the adjective.

A shell is a hard outer layer that covers and protects what is inside, as on an egg or a nut. Food makers borrow the word for a coating they build around a filling. The shell of milk chocolate here is there to stop water getting in or out.

Used as a noun, a spread is a soft paste you smear on bread, like butter, jam or peanut butter. Biscoff spread is the biscuit crushed into a paste of exactly that kind. The word is a sense trap, because spread as a verb simply means to move out across something.

A crumb is a tiny broken piece of bread, cake or biscuit. Bakers also use crumb for the soft crumbly inside of a baked thing, which is the sense here: the biscuit crumb is the biscuit material inside the bar. Keeping that crumb dry is the whole engineering problem.

To preserve something is to keep it as it is and stop it changing or decaying. Food can be preserved by freezing, drying, salting or sealing it. The fat layer in the bar was put there to preserve the biscuit's crunch, meaning to keep it crunchy for months.

Shelf life is how long a food is supposed to stay good while it sits on a shelf. It is what the date printed on a package is about. Best before is a promise about quality, so the food is usually still safe afterwards, while use by on things like milk and meat is the promise about safety.

To hold, in this sense, is to stay as it is without giving way: a rope holds, a roof holds, a lead holds until the final whistle. Saying the texture held over its shelf life means it stayed crunchy for the whole time rather than slowly collapsing. Nobody is holding anything in their hands.

A complexity is a complicated detail that makes something harder than it looks. The plural points at a pile of such details rather than one big obstacle. Such complexities here means all the fiddly physics of keeping crunchy and soft in the same bar.

To keep up with something is to move fast enough not to fall behind it. You can keep up with a runner, with homework, or with demand. Foodmakers struggling to keep up with public interest means shoppers want textured snacks faster than companies can invent them.

To indulge is to let yourself have something purely because you enjoy it, so an indulgent food is a treat rather than a necessity. Texture-indulgent snacks are ones you eat for the pleasure of the crunch or chew itself. The hyphen just ties the two words into one description.

In economics, demand means how much of something people want to buy at a given moment, added up across everyone. It is not a demand in the sense of an order someone shouts. Demand for texture-rich snacks jumping 28% means shoppers wanted a lot more of them than before.

Supply is the partner of demand: how much of something is actually available for people to buy. When demand climbs faster than supply, shoppers want more than exists, and prices usually rise. Here demand rose 28% while supply rose only 8%, so most of that extra appetite went unmet.

Sales volume is how many units of something were sold, counted as actual items or weight rather than money. It is a useful measure because money totals go up when prices rise even if nobody buys more. Using volume to measure supply tells you how much textured snack food genuinely reached shoppers.

GLP-1 drugs, sold under names like Ozempic and Wegovy, copy a hormone the gut releases after a meal, so the body behaves as though it has already eaten. People taking them feel full sooner and eat less. They have spread fast enough that food companies now worry about selling to customers with smaller appetites.

Your appetite is how much you want to eat. The word also stretches to wanting anything strongly, as in an appetite for risk or an appetite for attention. The article uses both senses: drugs that shrink patients' appetites, and a general hunger for texture.

Sensory means to do with the senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch. A sensory hit is a burst of information arriving through several of them at once. The point is that a snack reaches you through sound and feel as well as flavour.

Product theatre is a marketing term for the show a product puts on when you use it: the hiss of a can opening, the snap of a bar breaking. None of it changes the ingredients, but it changes how the moment feels. Companies design that show deliberately, the way a stage play is designed.

To be glued to something is to be unable to look away from it, as though stuck there. People are glued to a screen, a window or a game. Nobody is actually attached to anything, and it is one of the few metaphors here that stays harmless.

A consumer is a person who buys and uses things, which is the name economists and companies use for ordinary shoppers. The word treats you by your role in the economy rather than as a student or a neighbour. Young consumers here means young people doing the buying.

To take note of something is to notice it and treat it as worth acting on. Saying brands have taken note means companies saw what was happening on social media and changed what they do. It is stronger than merely noticing and weaker than announcing a plan.

A brand is a name and image attached to a product so shoppers recognise it and expect the same thing every time: Oreo, Skittles, Nike. One company can own dozens of brands that seem to compete with each other. Here brands stands in for the companies behind them.

Adverts is the British short form of advertisements, where Americans say ads or commercials. Advert can also be a verb meaning to refer to something, but that use is rare and formal. Here they are simply the ads brands make to sell snacks.

To induce something is to bring it about or cause it to happen, usually a state or a feeling: sleep, panic, laughter. Doctors induce labour; a dull lecture induces yawning. Adverts designed to induce ASMR are built to trigger that tingly feeling on purpose.

ASMR stands for autonomous sensory meridian response, a long name for a simple thing: the pleasant tingly feeling some people get down the neck and scalp from quiet sounds like whispering, tapping or crunching. Not everyone experiences it. Huge numbers of videos exist purely to set it off, which is why food brands started copying their sounds.

To rack up something is to pile up a large total of it, bit by bit: points, debts, views, air miles. It comes from keeping score on a rack. Posts racked up 1.5bn views means all those posts added together reached that total.

Crunchtok is a hashtag used on TikTok for videos of people eating loud, crunchy food close to a microphone. The tok ending comes from the app's name and now gets stuck onto any topic that has a corner there, as in booktok. A tag like this is how a whole genre of video gets a name.

bn is the standard short form for billion in British writing, the way m stands for million and trn for trillion. So 1.5bn views means one and a half billion, or 1,500,000,000. The Economist uses these abbreviations throughout its pages to save space.

For its part is a way of turning to one side of a story after describing another: shoppers want this, and the industry, for its part, wants that. It signals a change of viewpoint rather than disagreement. You will also meet for my part and for their part.

To differentiate is to tell things apart or make them different. In business, differentiation means whatever makes your product distinct from a rival's, so shoppers have a reason to pick it: price, flavour, a brand name, now texture. Saying texture is the last remaining form of differentiation means companies have run out of other ways to stand out.

A peak is the highest point of something, like a mountain top or the peak of a career. Writers now put peak in front of a noun to mean the most of that thing there will ever be: peak oil, peak traffic. Peak taste means flavour has gone as far as it can go, with nothing new left to find.

To venture is to go somewhere or try something that carries a risk. You venture out in a storm or venture a guess. Without venturing into the unappetising means companies could invent new flavours, but only strange ones nobody wants to eat.

Something unappetising does not make you want to eat it. The root is appetite, so appetising food looks and smells good and unappetising food does the opposite. The British spelling uses an s where American English would write unappetizing.

All manner of something means every kind of it, with manner carrying its older sense of sort or type. It is a touch more formal than all kinds of. Chocolate in all manner of formats means chocolate sold in every shape and package you can think of.

A format is the shape, size or arrangement something comes in, separate from what it actually is. The same film exists in several formats and the same chocolate exists as a bar, a mini bar or a bag. Companies invent new formats because the format alone can make shoppers buy.

Mindless means done without thinking about it, almost automatically. Mindless scrolling, mindless chatter, mindless snacking. The article means people often eat a whole bag without noticing, because their attention is on a screen.

To binge is to do a lot of something in one stretch, far more than usual. It started out describing eating and drinking, then spread to television once whole series arrived at once. To binge a TV series is to watch episode after episode in a single sitting.

A nutritionist studies nutrition, which is how food affects the body and what it needs to stay healthy. Food companies employ them to advise on what goes into products and how it will be received. The one quoted here works for Mondelez.

To liken one thing to another is to say they are alike, drawing a comparison on purpose. It is the verb hiding inside the word like. She likens texture-rich snacks to a film in 3D, meaning both take something ordinary and make the experience feel bigger.

To tire of something is to grow bored with it and stop wanting it, which has nothing to do with the tires on a car. You tire of a song after hearing it too often. Big food hopes shoppers do not tire of texture the way they tired of new flavours.

Crunch time is the moment when pressure peaks and something has to be decided or delivered: the last minute of a game, the night before a deadline. The article ends on a pun, because the crunch snack companies want in their products is not the crunch they would face if shoppers lost interest. A crunch in this sense is a squeeze or a crisis.
